items.title: Measles elimination at risk—and what a Florida study shows about Pfizer's COVID vaccine
items.summary: A Florida study comparing deaths after the Pfizer and Moderna COVID vaccines is getting a lot of attention, and one statistic from it is filling the echo chambers: a 40% higher rate of death with Pfizer. This edition closes with a closer look at that number and why it doesn't show that the vaccine caused deaths.
items.t: Measles elimination at risk—and what a Florida study shows about Pfizer's COVID vaccine

items.title: Brain atlas reveals how aging unfolds differently across brain regions, cell types and sexes
items.summary: How do we age, and how do we become more at risk of brain diseases as we age? An Arizona State University-led team is helping answer those questions with a new high-resolution atlas of the aging primate brain.
items.t: Brain atlas reveals how aging unfolds differently across brain regions, cell types and sexes

items.title: Intensified liver-directed radionuclide therapy shows promise for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors
items.summary: Combining intraarterial and intravenous administration of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) can selectively intensify treatment for liver-dominant metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) while still effectively delivering treatment throughout the whole body. This hybrid approach safely delivered over three times more radiation directly to liver metastases, resulting in encouraging tumor responses among patients. This research was published online in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine.
items.t: Intensified liver-directed radionuclide therapy shows promise for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors

items.title: Where will Ebola spread next? Travel patterns offer clues
items.summary: How many trips have you squeezed into the past 10 days? Whether you're in Boston or across the globe, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, your daily routine keeps you on the move. Between seven work commutes, a couple of grocery runs, a pharmacy stop and weekend dinner with friends, you can cover a lot of ground.
items.t: Where will Ebola spread next? Travel patterns offer clues

items.title: Scientists breed a 'pan-African' malaria parasite to build a better whole-parasite malaria vaccine
items.summary: Researchers have created a hybrid malaria parasite that combines the manufacturing advantages of the strain used in every current whole-parasite malaria vaccine with the much higher liver infectivity of a parasite collected recently in East Africa. The work is published in JCI Insight.
items.t: Scientists breed a 'pan-African' malaria parasite to build a better whole-parasite malaria vaccine

McMurrin Chair, proposed in a recent paper a new approach to understanding immunity for both experts and nonexperts, which could help address vaccine hesitancy in a science-leery public.
items.t: Q&A: Rethinking immunity beyond 'strong' and 'weak'

items.title: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
items.summary: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.
items.t: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults

items.title: Hamster hibernation study offers clues to Alzheimer's disease
items.summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have discovered that hibernation triggers changes in brain cells that partially resemble those in Alzheimer's disease. Studying golden hamsters, the team identified changes in gene expression across the hibernation cycle, which resemble those associated with the accumulation of amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's.

items.summary: Vitamin D may help the body fight influenza by controlling inflammation and the amount of virus in the lungs, according to a study in mice led by researchers at Penn State.

items.title: Human-to-human hantavirus spread confirmed on cruise ship
items.summary: In April 2026, an outbreak of severe respiratory infections, presenting as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), was detected aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius, which had left Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. items.t: Does a heart stent prevent future heart attacks in stable patients? 25-year follow-up offers new insight

items.title: Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
items.summary: Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.

items.title: STAT+: Senators introduce bill to curb conflicts of interest on preventive care panel
items.summary:
WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services.

The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest.

The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year. 

Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
items.t: STAT+: Senators introduce bill to curb conflicts of interest on preventive care panel

items.title: Label-free imaging tracks lipid storage in living liver organoids
items.summary: Fat accumulation in liver cells is central to several metabolic disorders, but observing the process in living tissue models remains difficult. Fluorescent labels and stains can provide detailed images, but they may disrupt cells or capture only selected time points. A label-free approach for tracking changes in lipid storage over time in three-dimensional mouse liver organoids is reported in Biophotonics Discovery.

items.title: Stomach cancer is changing: An expert explains surgical approaches
items.summary: Sometimes innovation in cancer care means developing something entirely new. Other times, it means returning to an old idea with the knowledge and tools to make it work better. Both are happening in stomach cancer surgery, says Travis Grotz, M.D., a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist who specializes in treating stomach cancer.

items.title: How the brain rapidly learns to interpret ambiguous images
items.summary: Both humans and image recognition algorithms can take time to identify the objects and scenes depicted in some images. Emblematic examples of this phenomenon are Mooney images, pictures that are intentionally reduced to patches of black and white, with no shades of gray.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
items.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

items.title: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
items.summary: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.
items.t: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

items.title: Despite programs for firefighter health, most rural firefighters are left behind

items.title: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch
items.summary: A major study of nearly 1,900 older adults suggests that stopping statins after age 70 may be relatively safe in the short term for people who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke. However, a higher rate of serious cardiovascular events or death during longer follow-up raises questions about the risks of discontinuing these widely prescribed medications.

items.title: Taking a closer look at stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation
items.summary: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), one of the most common heart rhythm disorders, are at increased risk of ischemic stroke, a stroke caused by a blood clot blocking blood flow to the brain, as well as blood clots that can travel to other parts of the body.

items.title: New test identifies people at higher risk of glaucoma, the leading cause of irreversible blindness

items.summary:
This is the second of two pieces about the experiencing of pre-clinical Alzheimer’s. Read the first here . 

In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “ The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease ” with this notably qualified call to action:

“In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.”

items.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

items.title: STAT+: Scientists debut map of basal ganglia, a key brain region involved in an array of diseases
items.summary:
A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has shelved the fast-track drug review initiative launched during the Trump administration by former Commissioner Marty Makary , Reuters reports. Launched in June 2025, the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program aimed to slash drug review timelines to just one to two months ​for therapies addressing national priorities, such as urgent unmet health needs. But critics pointed to possible preferential treatment for companies meeting demands of President Trump, such as offering ‌drugs at lower prices. items.t: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.
items.t: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

items.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.
items.t: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

items.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
items.summary: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.
items.t: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

items.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
items.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.
items.t: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

items.title: Senior doctors call off two-day strike planned this month
items.summary: Consultants in England were due to walk out on 25 November in disputes over pay and working conditions.
items.t: Senior doctors call off two-day strike planned this month

items.title: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts
items.summary: Ancient manuscripts, including the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, have revealed traces of a deadly sheep virus whose history stretches back more than 3,700 years. Scientists discovered that the virus has remained remarkably unchanged for millennia, turning historic parchment into an unexpected record of ancient disease outbreaks.
items.t: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

items.title: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review
items.summary: Baroness Casey criticises variability of services and fees charged to self-funders in England.
items.t: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review

items.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
items.summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.
items.t: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

items.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
items.summary: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.
items.t: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

items.title: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
items.summary: Three pills came top and outperformed Prozac for preventing relapse in a large number of patients.
items.t: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds

items.title: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds
items.summary: A major review of more than 350 studies suggests that eating less protein could slow aging, improve metabolic health, and potentially extend lifespan, challenging the widespread belief that more protein is always better. Researchers warn that many sedentary adults may be consuming too much protein, while emphasizing that individual needs depend on age and physical activity.
items.t: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

items.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
items.summary: Even when bad cholesterol is brought down to healthy levels, some people remain at risk of heart attacks, and scientists may have discovered why. Researchers identified two types of fat-carrying particles that appear to promote inflammation and damage blood vessels through mechanisms beyond cholesterol buildup.
items.t: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

items.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.
items.t: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

items.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.
items.t: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
items.summary: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

items.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
items.summary: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.
items.t: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

items.title: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a buildup of a protein called Miro1 may be a hidden driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes, with preclinical experiments showing that removing it restores the muscles’ response to insulin. Exercise was also found to lower Miro1 levels in people with diabetes, revealing a potential new pathway for treating the disease.
items.t: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

items.title: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
items.summary: The theory of ‘Love Languages’ has no scientific origin but it's often still mentioned in modern dating.
items.t: What's your love language - and does it actually mean anything?
